title: Memory, GC & Low-Memory Handling
scopeHtml: Scope: per-app heap limits, ART garbage collection, bitmap and native memory, onTrimMemory, the low memory killer, leak mechanics at platform level, and OOM kinds. LeakCanary / profiler workflows belong to A6; process importance classes belong to the P2 chunk.

questions.promptHtml: Why does an Android app get an OutOfMemoryError when the phone still has gigabytes of free RAM? How do you find out your app's heap limit at runtime?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests whether you know the Java heap is capped per app by the OS, independent of physical RAM. Juniors assume "OOM = phone out of memory".

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Every app process gets a hard cap on its managed (ART) Java heap, set per device by system properties, not by free RAM. When the heap hits that cap and a GC can't free enough, ART throws OutOfMemoryError even if the device has plenty free. I read it with ActivityManager.getMemoryClass() (MB) or Runtime.getRuntime().maxMemory() (bytes). It is typically 128 to 512 MB on modern phones and much lower on old or low-RAM devices, so I never hardcode sizes.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
The cap exists so one app cannot starve the system and so the low memory killer (LMK) has predictable processes to reclaim.

  • dalvik.vm.heapgrowthlimit is the normal cap. getMemoryClass() returns it in MB. Runtime.maxMemory() returns the same limit in bytes (without largeHeap).
  • dalvik.vm.heapsize is the larger cap used when the manifest sets android:largeHeap="true". getLargeMemoryClass() returns it.
  • dalvik.vm.heapstartsize, heapminfree, heapmaxfree, heaptargetutilization shape how the heap grows between start and cap. The heap does not start at the cap; it grows as the allocator needs and GC targets a utilization (default around 0.75 in AOSP).
  • Values are OEM and device specific. I have seen 48 to 64 MB on old low-end devices and 256 to 512 MB on current flagships. Treat any number I quote as "typical, verify on the device".
Physical RAM 8 GB (free: 3 GB)
 |
 +-- Process A (your app)  Java heap cap = 256 MB   <-- OOM here even though 3 GB are free
 +-- Process B             ...

Important: the cap applies to the Java heap only. Native allocations (malloc, and bitmap pixels from Android 8.0 / API 26) are not under this cap, but they are still under device-wide pressure and LMK.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
val am = getSystemService(ActivityManager::class.java)
val classMb = am.memoryClass                       // heapgrowthlimit in MB
val largeMb = am.largeMemoryClass                  // heapsize in MB (needs largeHeap=true to use)
val maxBytes = Runtime.getRuntime().maxMemory()    // current cap in bytes
val used = Runtime.getRuntime().let { it.totalMemory() - it.freeMemory() }
val lowRam = am.isLowRamDevice                     // true on Android Go style devices
Log.d("MEM", "class=$classMb MB large=$largeMb MB max=${maxBytes shr 20} MB used=${used shr 20} MB lowRam=$lowRam")

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Sizing caches as "10% of device RAM". Size from memoryClass or maxMemory().
  • Believing largeHeap is a fix. It raises the Java cap only, and costs more GC work and more kill risk (see the largeHeap question).
  • Reading totalMemory() as "memory used". It is the current heap size; used = total - free.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does the cap also limit bitmap pixels? → Not since 8.0 (API 26): pixel data is in the native heap. Before that (3.0 to 7.1) pixels lived in the Java heap and counted.
  2. Is maxMemory() the same on every phone with the same RAM? → No. It depends on OEM properties and screen density; two 4 GB phones can differ by 2x.
  3. If the Java heap is under the cap, can the app still be killed for memory? → Yes. LMK kills by system-wide pressure and process importance, with no relation to your Java cap.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "heap limit is 256 MB, use largeHeap." Senior: names the properties, knows the cap is Java-only, sizes caches from memoryClass/isLowRamDevice, and separates "Java OOM" from "LMK kill" in crash telemetry.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A photo app hardcoded a 100 MB in-memory cache; fine on test flagships (cap 512 MB), instant OOMs on 192 MB devices.

questions.promptHtml: What does android:largeHeap="true" actually do, and when would you refuse to add it in a code review?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Separates people who treat it as a free OOM fix from people who understand it just moves the ceiling and has costs.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: largeHeap asks the system to use the larger dalvik.vm.heapsize cap instead of heapgrowthlimit for my process's Java heap. It is a request, not a guarantee, and on many devices the two values are equal. The costs are longer GC cycles on a bigger heap and a larger footprint that makes my process a better LMK victim. I only accept it for apps with a genuinely huge working set, such as a photo or video editor, and only after profiling shows the memory is justified.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Without it: cap = getMemoryClass() MB. With it: cap = getLargeMemoryClass() MB.
  • It does not help native or graphics memory. Since API 26 bitmap pixels are native, so largeHeap does nothing for them.
  • Larger heap means each collection has more live objects to mark and more fragmentation to manage. Concurrent copying GC keeps pauses short, but total GC CPU time and allocation stalls rise.
  • A bigger resident footprint raises the chance LMK kills the process when the user is in another app. Result: slower relaunch (cold start) and lost in-memory state.
  • It masks leaks. A leak that would crash in 5 minutes under a 192 MB cap crashes in 15 under 512 MB, which is harder to reproduce and worse for debugging.
Normal:       |==== heapgrowthlimit (e.g. 256 MB) ====|
largeHeap:    |==== heapsize        (e.g. 512 MB)  ========|
              ^ OOM here without it                ^ OOM here with it

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
<application
    android:largeHeap="true"
    ... />
// Verify you actually got more
val am = getSystemService(ActivityManager::class.java)
Log.d("MEM", "normal=${am.memoryClass}MB large=${am.largeMemoryClass}MB max=${Runtime.getRuntime().maxMemory() shr 20}MB")

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Adding it as the first reaction to an OOM crash instead of taking a heap dump.
  • Assuming it applies to the whole process memory. Java heap only.
  • Testing on a device where memoryClass == largeMemoryClass, seeing no difference, and concluding it is harmless.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What would you do instead for a big image editor? → Tile or downsample, reuse bitmaps via a pool, decode with ImageDecoder.setTargetSize, keep pixels native/hardware, and process in strips.
  2. How can you tell the flag took effect? → Compare Runtime.maxMemory() against memoryClass.
  3. Can the OS ignore it? → Yes; it is a hint. Low-RAM devices may not have a larger value to offer.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "gives more memory, use it if OOM." Senior: explains the mechanism, side effects on GC and LMK, how it hides leaks, and proposes structural alternatives.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team shipped largeHeap to "fix" OOMs; the OOM rate fell 30% but cold-start rate rose and background kills doubled because the app was now the biggest cached process.

questions.promptHtml: Name the different kinds of memory an Android app process uses, and which of them are limited by the Java heap cap.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: The most common memory confusion: people watch only the Java heap and miss native and graphics growth.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A process has the ART Java heap (my objects, capped), the native heap (malloc, C++ libraries, and bitmap pixels from 8.0), graphics memory (GPU textures, surface buffers, hardware bitmaps), code (mapped dex, oat/vdex, .so files), thread stacks, and other mmapped files. Only the Java heap has the per-app cap. The whole process is still subject to device pressure and LMK.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
dumpsys meminfo <pkg> reports these rows, which map directly to the categories:

Row What it is Capped by heap limit?
Java Heap ART managed objects (Kotlin/Java) Yes
Native Heap malloc/new, libc, NDK, bitmap pixels (API 26+), direct ByteBuffers No
Code mapped .dex/.oat/.vdex/.so/.jar No
Stack thread stacks No
Graphics GL/Vulkan buffers, textures, gralloc, hardware bitmaps No
Private Other ashmem/memfd, mapped fonts, misc No
System shared system memory attributed to you No

Typical healthy split for a mid-size app: Java 40 to 120 MB, Native 30 to 100 MB, Graphics 50 to 200 MB depending on screen size and image use. These are rough ranges, not limits.

The consequence: an app can have a 60 MB Java heap, 500 MB total PSS, and get LMK-killed, while its Java OOM dashboard is clean.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
adb shell dumpsys meminfo com.example.app
adb shell dumpsys meminfo -a com.example.app   # more detail
val mi = Debug.MemoryInfo()
Debug.getMemoryInfo(mi)
val stats = mi.memoryStats           // keys: summary.java-heap, summary.native-heap, summary.graphics, ...
Log.d("MEM", stats.toString())

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using Runtime.totalMemory() as the whole app footprint.
  • Blaming the Java heap for a growth that is really in Graphics (e.g., unbounded texture/bitmap use).
  • Treating "Native Heap" as C++ only; bitmap pixels from 8.0 are in there too.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Where do hardware bitmaps show up? → In graphics memory, not Java or native heap.
  2. Why does Code memory matter? → Mapped file pages are shared and reclaimable, so they are cheap compared with anonymous dirty memory.
  3. Which category is the usual cause of "memory grows but Java heap flat"? → Native heap (direct buffers, JNI leaks, bitmaps) or Graphics.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "Java heap and native heap." Senior: lists all categories, ties each to a meminfo row, and says which are capped and which can silently grow.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A video-thumbnail screen kept 4K frames as Bitmaps: Java heap flat at 70 MB, Native 700 MB, silent LMK kills, nothing in Crashlytics.

questions.promptHtml: How much memory does a decoded bitmap take, and where does that memory live? Why can a 200 KB JPEG blow up a low-end phone?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Bitmap sizing is the number one real-world memory topic. The math must be automatic.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Memory is width x height x bytes per pixel, independent of file size. ARGB_8888 is 4 bytes per pixel, so a 4000x3000 photo is 12,000,000 x 4 = 48,000,000 bytes, about 45.8 MiB, even if the JPEG file is 2 MB. From Android 8.0 the pixel buffer is in native memory (tracked so GC still reacts); on 3.0 to 7.1 it was in the Java heap. Drawable resources can also be scaled up by density at decode time.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Config sizes: ARGB_8888 = 4 B, RGB_565 = 2 B (no alpha), RGBA_F16 = 8 B, ALPHA_8 = 1 B, HARDWARE = GPU resident.
  • Compressed file size only matters for storage and network. Decoded size is what RAM pays.
  • Density scaling trap: a PNG put in drawable-mdpi and loaded on a 480 dpi (xxhdpi) device is scaled by 480/160 = 3 per axis, so memory grows 9x. A 1000x1000 mdpi image becomes 3000x3000 x 4 = 36,000,000 bytes (34.3 MiB). Put assets in the right bucket or drawable-nodpi, and use BitmapFactory.Options.inScaled=false if needed.
  • Where it lives:
    • API < 11: native. API 11 to 25: Java heap (so it counted toward the cap). API 26+: native heap via NativeAllocationRegistry, so allocation pressure still triggers GC.
  • Reduce by downsampling at decode: inSampleSize (powers of 2) or ImageDecoder.setTargetSize (API 28+), then load only the size the ImageView shows.
JPEG 2 MB on disk  --decode-->  12,000,000 px x 4 B = 45.8 MiB in RAM
display ImageView 360x270 only needs 97,200 px x 4 B = 0.37 MiB

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// API 28+: decode directly at target size
val src = ImageDecoder.createSource(file)
val bmp = ImageDecoder.decodeBitmap(src) { decoder, info, _ ->
    val scale = minOf(1f, 1080f / maxOf(info.size.width, info.size.height))
    decoder.setTargetSize((info.size.width * scale).toInt(), (info.size.height * scale).toInt())
}

// Pre-28 / BitmapFactory: two-pass with inSampleSize
val o = BitmapFactory.Options().apply { inJustDecodeBounds = true }
BitmapFactory.decodeFile(path, o)
o.inSampleSize = Integer.highestOneBit(maxOf(o.outWidth / 1080, 1))
o.inJustDecodeBounds = false
val small = BitmapFactory.decodeFile(path, o)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Estimating from file size.
  • Assets in drawable-mdpi only, upscaled on high density devices.
  • Calling recycle() out of habit; since 3.0 it rarely matters, and recycling a bitmap still on screen crashes ("Canvas: trying to use a recycled bitmap").

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What does Bitmap.getAllocationByteCount() vs getByteCount() give? → Allocation count is the real buffer size (can exceed byte count when a bitmap was reused with a larger one); use it for cache accounting.
  2. Can you cut memory without lowering visible quality? → Use RGB_565 for opaque photos where banding is acceptable, or hardware bitmaps, or downsample to display size.
  3. Is there a hard limit on drawing size? → Yes, the render pipeline throws when a bitmap above about 100 MB is drawn (RecordingCanvas limit).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "bitmaps use a lot of memory, use Glide." Senior: does the math aloud, names the density trap, states the API-level storage change, and explains what image libraries do internally (sampling, pools, caches).

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A banner PNG 1080x1920 placed in drawable-mdpi was decoded at 3x per axis on 99 devices of the test pool; 9x cost produced OOM only on high-density devices.

questions.promptHtml: Explain onTrimMemory levels. What should an app actually release at each level, and how is it different from onLowMemory?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Knowing the callback exists is junior. Knowing which resources to drop at which signal, and that the signal is advisory, is senior.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: onTrimMemory(level) is a ComponentCallbacks2 hint from the system that it wants processes to shed memory. TRIM_MEMORY_UI_HIDDEN (20) means my UI is no longer visible, so I drop view-related caches. The RUNNING_* levels (5, 10, 15) say I'm still in the foreground but the device is getting tight. The BACKGROUND/MODERATE/COMPLETE levels (40, 60, 80) say I'm cached and how close I am to being killed. It's advisory; LMK may kill me anyway. onLowMemory is the older coarse version, roughly the "complete" case.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Level Value Meaning Typical action
TRIM_MEMORY_RUNNING_MODERATE 5 foreground, system starting to get low trim non-essential caches
TRIM_MEMORY_RUNNING_LOW 10 foreground, low shrink image cache, stop prefetching
TRIM_MEMORY_RUNNING_CRITICAL 15 foreground, critical, background processes already being killed release almost everything non-visible
TRIM_MEMORY_UI_HIDDEN 20 all UI hidden drop UI-only resources (view caches, big bitmaps for screens)
TRIM_MEMORY_BACKGROUND 40 cached, near the start of LRU list release what is cheap to rebuild
TRIM_MEMORY_MODERATE 60 cached, middle of LRU list release more
TRIM_MEMORY_COMPLETE 80 cached, next kill candidate release everything rebuildable

Version note: several of these constants are marked deprecated in recent API levels (I recall the background-list ones around API 34 and the RUNNING_* ones around API 35, with the system no longer sending some of them). Verify on developer.android.com for the target API; TRIM_MEMORY_UI_HIDDEN remains the dependable, always-sent signal.

Where to receive it: Application, Activity, Service and ContentProvider implement ComponentCallbacks2. Anywhere else: context.registerComponentCallbacks(...). For caches, register once at app level so every cache hears it.

onLowMemory() predates it; it fires when the whole system is low, equivalent to asking for maximum release.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class App : Application() {
    override fun onTrimMemory(level: Int) {
        super.onTrimMemory(level)
        when {
            level >= ComponentCallbacks2.TRIM_MEMORY_COMPLETE -> ImageCache.clear()
            level >= ComponentCallbacks2.TRIM_MEMORY_BACKGROUND -> ImageCache.trimToSize(ImageCache.size() / 4)
            level >= ComponentCallbacks2.TRIM_MEMORY_UI_HIDDEN -> ImageCache.trimToSize(ImageCache.size() / 2)
        }
    }
}
# Test without waiting for real pressure
adb shell am send-trim-memory com.example.app RUNNING_CRITICAL
adb shell am send-trim-memory com.example.app BACKGROUND

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using level == X instead of >= on the numeric ordering when intending "at least this severe".
  • Doing heavy work (rebuilding caches) in the callback, which runs on the main thread.
  • Believing that releasing memory here prevents the kill. It only lowers the footprint, which may move you down the kill list.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why use UI_HIDDEN instead of onStop? → UI_HIDDEN triggers on the whole process's UI going away (all activities), while onStop is per-activity and fires during normal transitions between your own screens.
  2. Is it guaranteed to be delivered before a kill? → No. Kill can happen without any callback.
  3. How would you test the whole path? → am send-trim-memory, assert caches shrink, and verify via dumpsys meminfo before and after.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "release caches in onTrimMemory." Senior: ties levels to process state, avoids heavy work in the callback, notes deprecations, registers at app level, and tests it with adb.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A feed app released its decoded-bitmap cache on UI_HIDDEN and cut background kills of its process by about a quarter on 2 GB devices.

questions.promptHtml: In dumpsys meminfo, what do PSS, RSS, Private Dirty and USS mean, and which one do you trust to decide whether your app is "too big"?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Reading memory numbers wrongly leads to chasing noise. Shared pages make naive sums wrong.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: RSS counts every resident page the process maps, including pages shared with other processes, so it over-counts. PSS (proportional set size) divides shared pages among the processes that share them, so summing PSS across processes works. USS (unique set size) is only the private pages, which is what would be freed if the process died. For "how much does my app really cost", I use PSS for comparison and Private Dirty/USS for "what would a kill reclaim".

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Example. Process X has 100 MB of private pages and maps 60 MB of shared libraries that 3 processes (X, Y, Z) all use.

  • RSS(X) = 100 + 60 = 160 MB.
  • PSS(X) = 100 + 60/3 = 120 MB.
  • USS(X) = 100 MB. Sum of PSS across X, Y, Z gives total physical use without double counting; sum of RSS would count the 60 MB shared three times.

meminfo columns:

  • Pss Total: proportional.
  • Private Dirty: private pages that were modified; cannot be dropped without swapping or killing (Android has no regular disk swap; zRAM compresses instead).
  • Private Clean: unmodified private pages (like file-backed code), can be dropped and re-read.
  • Swap PSS: portion compressed into zRAM.

LMK decides on its own pressure heuristics, but practically the data that hurts you is Private Dirty (anon + dirty) because it can't be reclaimed cheaply.

           Process X
 [ private dirty 100 MB ][ shared libs 60 MB, shared by X,Y,Z ]
 RSS = 160   PSS = 120   USS = 100

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
adb shell dumpsys meminfo com.example.app            # summary + PSS per category
adb shell dumpsys meminfo -a com.example.app         # full, includes "Dalvik Other", "Ashmem"
adb shell cat /proc/$(adb shell pidof com.example.app)/smaps_rollup   # RSS, PSS, Private_Dirty rollup

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Comparing RSS before and after a fix and calling it a win while PSS is unchanged.
  • Measuring right after launch. Do a few GC cycles and a stable state; use System.gc() is not reliable, use profiler "force GC" for comparison.
  • Reading "TOTAL" of one category as the app's total.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why does the Android Studio profiler show a smaller number than meminfo TOTAL? → The profiler's memory graph categories are subsets (Java, Native, Graphics, Stack, Code, Others); totals use PSS and exclude some system-attributed shared memory.
  2. Does a bigger PSS mean the LMK kills it first? → Not alone. Oom adj (process importance) is first; PSS breaks ties among similar adj.
  3. What is zRAM's role? → Compressed in-RAM swap. Swap PSS shows pages sitting in it; touching them costs CPU to decompress.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "PSS is memory used by the app." Senior: gives the proportional math, uses Private Dirty as the reclaimable-by-kill number, and avoids RSS summation.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: An SDK team claimed "no memory cost" by showing RSS stayed flat; PSS and Private Dirty showed +40 MB because new anonymous pages replaced already-shared ones.

questions.promptHtml: How does garbage collection work on modern Android (ART)? What do the GC lines in logcat tell you, and when does GC actually hurt the UI?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Checks that you can reason about GC as a cost model instead of "GC is automatic, not my problem".

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: ART uses a mostly concurrent, compacting collector (concurrent copying since Android 8.0) that does most work on a background thread with very short pauses. GC hurts when I allocate faster than it reclaims. Then an allocation can block waiting for a GC ("GC_FOR_ALLOC"), or the GC thread steals CPU from the render path. I read the art log lines for cause, freed amount, heap utilization, and pause time to see which case I'm in.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Reachability model: objects reachable from GC roots (static fields, thread stacks, JNI references, class loaders) survive; everything else is garbage. No reference counting.
  • Collectors over history: Dalvik mark-sweep (stop-the-world, tens of ms pauses) → ART CMS (Android 5 to 7) → Concurrent Copying (CC) default from Android 8.0 (API 26). Newer releases add other collectors; see the ART internals question.
  • GC causes seen in logs: Alloc / GC_FOR_ALLOC (an allocation failed, so the allocating thread waits; the bad one), Background / Concurrent (heap crossed a threshold, GC runs on a daemon thread), Explicit (System.gc()), NativeAlloc (native allocation pressure, e.g., bitmaps), CollectorTransition, HeapTrim.
  • Typical line (format varies by release):
I/art: Background concurrent copying GC freed 41230(2MB) AllocSpace objects, 3(1MB) LOS objects,
       36% free, 38MB/60MB, paused 215us,402us total 61.2ms
I/art: Waiting for a blocking GC Alloc          <-- allocation had to wait: a red flag
I/art: Alloc concurrent copying GC freed ... paused 1.2ms total 48ms   <-- blocking GC on alloc
  • Reading it: "freed X(bytes) objects" = churn; "% free, used/total" = headroom (near the cap means pressure); "paused" = stop-the-world portions; "total" = wall-clock concurrent time.
  • Why GC jank is not about pauses anymore: pauses are typically sub-millisecond to a few ms. The visible cost is (1) blocking GC during allocation near the cap and (2) CPU contention on small cores while rendering at 60/90/120 Hz.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
adb logcat -s art:I dalvikvm:I              # GC lines
adb shell am dumpheap com.example.app /data/local/tmp/x.hprof
adb shell dumpsys meminfo com.example.app   # includes "Objects", "Views", "Activities" counts
// Cheap runtime signals
val rt = Runtime.getRuntime()
Log.d("GC", "used=${(rt.totalMemory() - rt.freeMemory()) shr 20}MB max=${rt.maxMemory() shr 20}MB")
Log.d("GC", "gcCount=${Debug.getRuntimeStat("art.gc.gc-count")} blocked=${Debug.getRuntimeStat("art.gc.blocking-gc-count")}")

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Calling System.gc() to "free memory". It triggers an explicit full collection and does not fix leaks.
  • Believing finalizers or WeakReference give predictable cleanup timing.
  • Assuming "no GC pauses in logs" means no GC jank; check allocation stalls and CPU.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What is a GC root? → Static fields, live thread stack locals, JNI global/local refs, class loader and system roots.
  2. Why do Dalvik-era GC tips (pooling everything) mostly not apply now? → Concurrent compaction made pauses tiny, so pool only hot, large, or churny objects.
  3. How do you see blocking GCs in production? → Debug.getRuntimeStat("art.gc.blocking-gc-count") and blocking-gc-time (API 23+) reported to telemetry.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "GC frees unused objects; avoid creating objects in loops." Senior: names the collector, distinguishes blocking vs background GC, reads the log line, and measures with runtime stats instead of guessing.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A chat list hit 1.5 s jank bursts on mid devices; logs showed repeated Alloc GCs at 95% heap use caused by a 40 MB cache plus a leak, not by "slow rendering".

questions.promptHtml: What is allocation churn, why does it cause jank even though the heap is not leaking, and what are the most common hidden allocations in Kotlin Android code?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Production perf bugs are often churn, not leaks. Probes knowledge of Kotlin boxing, lambdas, and per-frame code.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Churn is creating many short-lived objects rapidly. Nothing leaks, but the heap fills quickly, GC runs often, and on a busy main thread or a small CPU it competes with frame work. Hot paths such as onDraw, onBindViewHolder, scroll listeners, and per-item mapping are where it bites. Typical hidden allocators: boxing primitives in generic collections, string formatting and concatenation, capturing lambdas, Regex constructed in a loop, Paint/Rect created inside onDraw, and chained map/filter creating intermediate lists.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Budget example. A RecyclerView binding at 60 fps while flinging binds about 6 rows per frame in the worst case. If each bind allocates a formatted String (60 B), a SimpleDateFormat (about 1 KB internal state, not cheap), and 5 lambdas (about 24 B each), that is about 1.2 KB per row, 7.2 KB per frame, 430 KB/s. Small alone, but with a 20 MB young-ish headroom it triggers a collection every ~45 s of scroll plus bigger spikes when parsing happens. Add the SimpleDateFormat fix and it falls below 100 KB/s. The principle: find the top allocators, not guess.

Hidden allocators in Kotlin:

  • List<Int>, Map<Long, X>, Array<Int?>: each element boxed (Java Integer cache only covers -128..127).
  • Non-inline lambdas that capture variables allocate a closure object per call; inline functions avoid it.
  • "$a $b" builds a StringBuilder + String each time.
  • for (i in 0 until n) is optimized, but forEach on non-inline collections or .withIndex() may allocate iterators/pairs depending on form.
  • Regex("..."), Pattern.compile, DateTimeFormatter, Gson(), SimpleDateFormat: expensive to construct, cache them.
  • Defensive copies: list.toList(), copy() of big data classes in state reducers.

How to find them: Android Studio Memory Profiler "Record Java/Kotlin allocations" (sampled), or Perfetto Java heap sampling, and compare allocation count per frame.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// BAD: allocates a Paint and Rect every frame
override fun onDraw(c: Canvas) {
    val p = Paint(Paint.ANTI_ALIAS_FLAG).apply { color = Color.RED }
    val r = Rect(0, 0, width, height)
    c.drawRect(r, p)
}

// GOOD: hoist, mutate in place
private val paint = Paint(Paint.ANTI_ALIAS_FLAG).apply { color = Color.RED }
private val rect = Rect()
override fun onDraw(c: Canvas) {
    rect.set(0, 0, width, height)
    c.drawRect(rect, paint)
}
// Primitive-specialized collections avoid boxing
val counts = androidx.collection.MutableIntIntMap()  // or SparseIntArray / LongSparseArray

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Pooling everything. A pool of trivially small objects costs more complexity than the GC does.
  • Optimizing without a profile. Allocation is cheap in ART; only hot paths matter.
  • Moving allocations to a background thread and calling it fixed. Total GC pressure is the same.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Is Paint allocation in onDraw flagged by tools? → Android Lint warns (DrawAllocation).
  2. When is an object pool correct? → Large (bitmaps, big buffers), expensive to build, or in a measured hot loop.
  3. How do you prove improvement? → Allocation count and GC count/time per scenario run before and after, with a macrobenchmark or a repeatable scripted flow.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "avoid creating objects in onDraw." Senior: quantifies, lists Kotlin-specific hidden allocations, uses sampling tools, and warns against premature pooling.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A search screen allocating a Regex per keystroke per item (60 items) produced bursty GCs and visible typing lag on 3 GB devices.

questions.promptHtml: How does Android decide which process to kill under memory pressure, and how can you tell in production that your app was killed for memory rather than crashing?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: LMK kills leave no crash trace. Senior candidates know how to detect them.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Android keeps a score per process (oom_score_adj) that reflects importance: the foreground app is 0, visible about 100, perceptible about 200, services around 500, and cached processes 900+. The userspace daemon lmkd watches memory pressure (PSI based on devices with kernel support, older versions used free-memory thresholds) and kills the highest score first, which means cached background apps die first. A kill is a SIGKILL, so no exception or onDestroy. In production I use ApplicationExitInfo (API 30+) and look for REASON_LOW_MEMORY.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• ActivityManagerService computes adj per process from components (foreground activity, bound services, providers, FGS), and lmkd is told via a socket. Typical bands (AOSP values, vendor tuning may vary): native/persistent negative, FOREGROUND_APP 0, VISIBLE_APP 100, PERCEPTIBLE_APP 200, BACKUP 300, HEAVY_WEIGHT 400, SERVICE 500, HOME 600, PREVIOUS_APP 700, SERVICE_B 800, CACHED 900..999.
  • Within the same adj, larger processes are better victims, which is why footprint matters for background apps.
  • Since Android 10, lmkd can be PSI-based (kills when stalls from memory reclaim exceed thresholds); earlier it used minfree thresholds. OEMs often tune this aggressively.
  • A kill is not a crash: no Crashlytics event, no Thread.UncaughtExceptionHandler, no onSaveInstanceState after the fact. State must have been saved earlier (see process-death chunk).
  • Detection: ActivityManager.getHistoricalProcessExitReasons(pkg, 0, 5) (API 30+) returns ApplicationExitInfo with reason (REASON_LOW_MEMORY, REASON_ANR, REASON_CRASH, REASON_EXCESSIVE_RESOURCE_USAGE, REASON_USER_REQUESTED, ...), importance, pss, rss, and sometimes a trace.
oom adj   0 foreground    -> last to die
        100 visible
        200 perceptible (music FGS)
        500 service
       900+ cached        -> first to die (largest first among equals)

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
fun logPriorExits(ctx: Context) {
    val am = ctx.getSystemService(ActivityManager::class.java)
    am.getHistoricalProcessExitReasons(ctx.packageName, 0, 5).forEach { e ->
        Log.i("EXIT", "reason=${e.reason} importance=${e.importance} " +
            "pssKb=${e.pss} rssKb=${e.rss} desc=${e.description} ts=${e.timestamp}")
        // upload only reason / importance / pss buckets to telemetry
    }
}
adb shell am kill com.example.app          # simulates cached-process kill (only works when in background)
adb shell dumpsys activity processes | grep -A3 com.example.app   # see adj / state

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Expecting a crash report. LMK kills are silent.
  • Treating onTrimMemory as a guarantee you'll get a warning.
  • Using adb shell kill -9 and calling it a faithful simulation. am kill follows the "OS killed a cached process" path, which also preserves the saved state in the system.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What does an FGS do to the adj? → Promotes the process to perceptible/service-level importance, so it dies later than cached apps, not never.
  2. Can an app opt out of being killed? → No. Persistent system apps only. Reduce footprint and persist state.
  3. How do you separate OEM aggressive killing from LMK? → ApplicationExitInfo.reason and importance; OEM "force stop" shows as REASON_USER_REQUESTED or lacks one, and no trim levels precede it. Also compare by device manufacturer in telemetry.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "background apps get killed when low on memory." Senior: knows adj bands, lmkd behavior, silent nature of the kill, and uses ApplicationExitInfo for production attribution.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Support tickets said "app forgets my draft". Exit-info telemetry showed 60% of sessions ended as REASON_LOW_MEMORY at importance CACHED on 3 GB phones; fix was incremental draft persistence, not memory trimming.

questions.promptHtml: What exactly is a memory leak in a garbage-collected runtime? Walk me through why a leaked Activity is so expensive and the platform-level patterns that create them.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: A leak is "reachable but unneeded". A candidate who can't explain GC roots can't debug them.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: In a GC runtime a leak means an object I no longer need is still reachable from a GC root, so it is never collected. A leaked Activity keeps its entire view tree, any bitmaps in it, its ViewModel references, and anything captured by its listeners, so one leak often costs several MB. The common roots are static fields, singletons, long-lived threads, registered listeners and callbacks, and system services holding my objects.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Reachability chain example:

GC root: static field  Repo.INSTANCE
   -> Repo.callback (lambda)
        -> captured `this` = DetailActivity
              -> window decor view -> 300 views -> 6 bitmaps (14 MB)

Anything on this path stays alive. Cutting any link (clear the callback, use a WeakReference, bind to lifecycle) lets GC collect the whole subgraph.

Platform-level patterns:

  1. Static / singleton holding Context or View. companion object { var ctx: Context }, object Foo { lateinit var activity }. Use applicationContext for singletons.
  2. Non-static inner classes, anonymous classes, lambdas. Capture the outer this implicitly (Java inner class) or whatever the lambda uses (Kotlin lambdas capture only what they reference, this included if you touch a member).
  3. Registered but never unregistered: SensorManager, LocationManager, BroadcastReceiver, ContentObserver, Application.registerActivityLifecycleCallbacks, ViewTreeObserver listeners, LiveData.observeForever, Rx subscriptions.
  4. Long-running threads and Handlers. A Thread or posted delayed Message holds its Runnable until it finishes; the Message queue references the target Handler which references the Activity.
  5. ViewModel holding a View or Activity. ViewModel survives configuration change, so it pins the old Activity.
  6. Fragment view not nulled (binding field retained after onDestroyView). Owned by the Fragments chunk.
  7. Context-bound caches in libraries (e.g., WebView with an Activity context).

The cost multiplier: after rotation, a leaked old Activity and a new one coexist: two view trees, two sets of bitmaps. Repeat rotations leak linearly: 10 rotations x 8 MB = 80 MB.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Leaky: singleton holds Activity through a lambda
object Analytics { private var onEvent: (() -> Unit)? = null
    fun setListener(l: () -> Unit) { onEvent = l } }
class MainActivity : AppCompatActivity() {
    override fun onCreate(b: Bundle?) { super.onCreate(b)
        Analytics.setListener { title = "evt" }   // captures `this`
    }
}
// Fix: unregister in the matching lifecycle callback or use lifecycle-aware wiring
override fun onDestroy() { Analytics.setListener {}; super.onDestroy() }

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Assuming onDestroy clears things. It does not null references held elsewhere.
  • Believing WeakReference is always a fix; it hides lifecycle design problems and can cause "callback silently dropped" bugs.
  • Calling System.gc() to check for leaks; use heap dumps (covered in profiling/LeakCanary material).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does a Kotlin lambda always capture this? → Only if the lambda body references members or this. A lambda using only local vals captures those, not the Activity.
  2. How does the system itself cause leaks? → Framework bugs (historic ones in InputMethodManager, TextLine); AOSP references can pin contexts; libraries should pass applicationContext.
  3. Why do leaks matter after rotations specifically? → Each recreation allocates a new view tree while the old one is pinned; costs multiply with configuration changes.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "avoid static Context references." Senior: states the reachability model, draws the root-to-leak chain, enumerates platform patterns, and quantifies cost per leak.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A "settings" screen leaked via an observeForever call in a singleton repo; each visit pinned 6 MB, discovered only on Crashlytics OOM clusters from heavy users.

questions.contextHtml:
Code review for a DetailActivity in a shopping app (12M MAU, crash dashboard shows OOM at 3% of sessions, mostly on 3 GB devices). Heap dump shows 11 instances of DetailActivity alive after a user browsed 11 product pages and went back. Each instance retains about 9 MB (view tree plus product images).

object ImageBus {
    var current: Activity? = null
    val listeners = mutableListOf<(Bitmap) -> Unit>()
}

class DetailActivity : AppCompatActivity() {
    private lateinit var binding: ActivityDetailBinding
    private val sensorManager by lazy { getSystemService(SensorManager::class.java) }

    private val sensorListener = object : SensorEventListener {
        override fun onSensorChanged(e: SensorEvent) { binding.tilt.rotation = e.values[0] }
        override fun onAccuracyChanged(s: Sensor?, a: Int) {}
    }

    override fun onCreate(b: Bundle?) {
        super.onCreate(b)
        binding = ActivityDetailBinding.inflate(layoutInflater)
        setContentView(binding.root)
        ImageBus.current = this
        ImageBus.listeners.add { bmp -> binding.image.setImageBitmap(bmp) }
        sensorManager.registerListener(sensorListener,
            sensorManager.getDefaultSensor(Sensor.TYPE_ACCELEROMETER), SensorManager.SENSOR_DELAY_UI)
        Handler(Looper.getMainLooper()).postDelayed({ binding.title.text = "Sale ends" }, 10 * 60_000L)
    }
}
questions.promptHtml: Find every leak, say what reference chain keeps each Activity alive, quantify the damage, and fix it.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Spots only ImageBus.current (the obvious static) and says "use WeakReference". Misses the lambda in listeners, the sensor registration, and the 10-minute Handler message. Fixes one, and OOMs persist.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the Activity ever finished by back press vs process kept in task? (Determines when onDestroy runs.) Does ImageBus need to outlive screens? (Decides whether it exists at all.) Is the 3% OOM correlated with browse-depth sessions? (Confirms leak-per-visit.) Which min API? (Affects available tooling like lifecycleScope.)
  2. Immediate mitigation: Ship a hotfix that nulls ImageBus.current and removes listeners in onDestroy, and unregisters the sensor in onPause. Do not raise largeHeap as a stopgap, because it only delays the crash and hurts LMK behavior.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) ImageBus.current static field: root = static, directly retains Activity. (b) listeners list: lambda captures binding which holds the root view and thus the Activity context. (c) SensorManager holds sensorListener, which is an anonymous inner class capturing this@DetailActivity (for binding). The system service is process-wide, so it is a GC root path. (d) Pending Message for 10 minutes: Looper queue -> Message -> Runnable lambda -> binding -> Activity. Leak until the message fires, so up to 10 minutes per instance.
  4. How I'd verify each: Take a heap dump after 11 visits (Android Studio Memory Profiler, or adb shell am dumpheap), filter by DetailActivity, open "References" tree on one instance; the shortest GC-root path lists the first link. Fix and re-dump; the count must drop to 0 or 1 after GC. Also LeakCanary in debug builds to catch regressions.
  5. Root cause: Four independent paths from GC roots (static field, static list, system service, main Looper queue) into the Activity. Fixing one leaves three alive, so the count stays at 11.
  6. Fix:
// Delete ImageBus.current; replace listeners with lifecycle-scoped collection
lifecycleScope.launch {
    repeatOnLifecycle(Lifecycle.State.STARTED) {
        imageFlow.collect { binding.image.setImageBitmap(it) }
    }
}
// Sensor tied to visibility
override fun onResume() { super.onResume()
    sensorManager.registerListener(sensorListener, accel, SensorManager.SENSOR_DELAY_UI) }
override fun onPause()  { super.onPause(); sensorManager.unregisterListener(sensorListener) }
// Delayed work tied to lifecycle (cancelled automatically)
lifecycleScope.launch { delay(10 * 60_000L); binding.title.text = "Sale ends" }

Long term: expose product images via a ViewModel/Flow, never via global mutable state. 7. Prevention: LeakCanary on debug and internal builds; a lint check or review rule banning Activity/View/Context in object/companion fields; a CI instrumented test that opens and closes the screen 20 times and fails if LeakCanary's instrumentation-test assertions (leakcanary-android-instrumentation) report a retained Activity. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do (and why): I would not wrap everything in WeakReference (hides lifecycle bugs and drops events nondeterministically). I would not call System.gc() or enable largeHeap. I would not add applicationContext blindly to fix UI-bound listeners; UI updates need a lifecycle owner.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• The leak is gone but OOM persists at 1%. → Check bitmaps: are images decoded at full resolution? Check ViewModel caches and Glide/Coil cache size; the leak was one cause among several.
  • Do I still need onDestroy cleanup if I use lifecycleScope? → Not for coroutine work; it cancels with the lifecycle. Still needed for non-lifecycle-aware registries.
  • Would a retained ViewModel hold the Activity? → Only if you pass it one. ViewModels must not reference Views or Activities.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite of a catalog app: the team fixed the static Activity field, saw crashes drop 40%, declared victory. The sensor listener leak stayed hidden for months because it only showed on devices where the user rotated often. A weekly "open/close screen 50x" soak test finally exposed the remaining count.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Finds one leak, suggests WeakReference or largeHeap.
  • Hire: Finds all four, explains chains, fixes with lifecycle APIs, verifies with a heap dump.
  • Strong hire: Also quantifies (11 x 9 MB ≈ 99 MB), adds regression protection (LeakCanary, soak test, lint/review rule), and rejects workarounds with reasons.

questions.promptHtml: What is Bitmap.Config.HARDWARE, what does it save, and what breaks when you use it?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Real optimization knowledge with real production pitfalls: crashes on read, fd limits, unsupported drawing paths.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: From API 26, a hardware bitmap keeps its pixels only in graphics memory (GPU-accessible), not in the app's CPU-side memory. That saves the second copy the renderer otherwise makes when it uploads a software bitmap into a GPU texture, so it can roughly halve memory per image and removes upload cost at draw time. The price: the bitmap is immutable and its pixels cannot be read on the CPU, so getPixel, copyPixelsToBuffer, software Canvas drawing, and some libraries (Palette, blur, certain transformations) fail.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Normal bitmap: pixel buffer in native heap (API 26+). On first draw, RenderThread uploads it to a texture, so the same image costs RAM twice (CPU copy + GPU copy). Hardware bitmap: single GPU-side copy.
  • Graphics memory shows up under "Graphics" in dumpsys meminfo, not Java or Native heap, so your heap graphs may show a drop but total may not change dramatically if you also keep the software copy anywhere.
  • Restrictions:
    • Immutable; Bitmap.isMutable false.
    • getPixel(s), copyPixelsToBuffer, compress() on some paths: throw or fail. Use bitmap.copy(Bitmap.Config.ARGB_8888, false) first.
    • Cannot draw into a software canvas (Canvas(bitmap) created from a software bitmap and drawBitmap(hardwareBmp)): throws IllegalStateException/"Software rendering doesn't support hardware bitmaps".
    • Screenshot paths using View.draw(Canvas(bitmap)) of views that contain hardware bitmaps can fail the same way.
    • On Android 8.0 and 8.1, each hardware bitmap used file descriptors; thousands of them can hit the process FD limit. Image libraries cap how many they create (I recall Glide limits this; verify the exact threshold in their source/docs).
  • Opt-in: BitmapFactory.Options.inPreferredConfig = HARDWARE, ImageDecoder default allocator (hardware when allowed), or the library's flag (Coil allowHardware(true) default, Glide DecodeFormat/hardware config).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Coil: disable hardware for a request that needs pixel access (e.g. Palette)
imageView.load(url) {
    allowHardware(false)
    listener(onSuccess = { _, r -> Palette.from((r.drawable as BitmapDrawable).bitmap).generate() })
}

// Manual: convert only when you must read pixels
val readable = hardwareBmp.copy(Bitmap.Config.ARGB_8888, /* mutable = */ false)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Enabling globally and discovering at runtime that a feature (share image, blur, color extraction) crashes.
  • Comparing Java heap before/after and ignoring Graphics rows.
  • Forgetting that copy() allocates a full software buffer, momentarily increasing memory.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does hardware bitmap help animations? → Draw performance improves (no re-upload) but you still pay the memory of each frame image.
  2. What about Android 14+? → Behavior is similar; verify image library defaults and ImageDecoder allocator behavior on the target API.
  3. How would you roll this out safely? → Per-surface opt-in, remote flag, crash and memory monitoring by device tier (see the migration scenario in this chunk).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "hardware bitmaps use less memory." Senior: explains the double-copy model, lists the capabilities lost, and knows to opt out per request.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A color-extraction feature crashed only for users on image-heavy feed screens after a library upgrade quietly turned hardware bitmaps on by default.

questions.promptHtml: "OutOfMemoryError" in Crashlytics can mean very different things. List the distinct kinds of memory-related failure on Android, how to tell them apart from the message, and what each one implies about the fix.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Senior engineers triage by failure mode. Treating every OOM as "reduce bitmaps" wastes weeks.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: There are at least six: (1) Java heap exhaustion ("Failed to allocate a N byte allocation ... growth limit"), (2) thread creation failure ("pthread_create (1040KB stack) failed"), (3) native allocation failure (abort in native code, SIGABRT or SIGSEGV), (4) oversized draw ("trying to draw too large bitmap"), (5) resource exhaustion like file descriptors ("Too many open files"), and (6) silent LMK kill with no exception at all. Each has a different message, different telemetry, and a different fix.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Kind Typical signature What it means Fix direction
Java heap java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Failed to allocate a 14745616 byte allocation with 4194304 free bytes and 5MB until OOM, target footprint 201326592, growth limit 201326592 Live set near cap, request doesn't fit Reduce live set, big arrays, caches; find leaks
Thread/stack OutOfMemoryError: pthread_create (1040KB stack) failed: Try again Cannot create thread: virtual address space, per-process thread limits, or cgroup pid limit Bound thread pools; find thread leaks
JNI/native Could not allocate JNI Env, or native abort with Out of memory in tombstone native malloc/mmap failed Native profiling, fix native leaks
Draw size RuntimeException: Canvas: trying to draw too large(…bytes) bitmap Single bitmap above about 100 MB in a draw Downsample, tile
FD exhaustion java.io.IOException: Too many open files (EMFILE), also Could not allocate JNI Env-like symptoms Open sockets/files/hardware bitmaps leaked Close resources, use {}; check /proc/<pid>/fd
LMK kill No exception. ApplicationExitInfo.REASON_LOW_MEMORY System-wide pressure, your process picked Reduce footprint, persist state

How to read the Java OOM message: "N byte allocation with F free bytes and U until OOM". U is how far the heap is from the cap. If N is large (e.g., 14.7 MB), the immediate trigger is a large array or similar. If N is small (4 KB) and U is tiny, the app was already at the cliff and a trivial allocation tipped it; the culprit is the live set, not the last allocation. target footprint and growth limit equal means no headroom left to grow.

A 14,745,616-byte allocation is 1920 x 1920 x 4 bytes + a 16-byte array header: a Java int[]/byte[] of pixels, not bitmap pixel memory (which is native from API 26). That detail alone says "custom pixel processing code", not "image library".

Virtual address space (VA) matters for 32-bit processes: ~3 GB usable, thread stacks (1 MB reserved each by default on Java threads), mapped files and the Java heap all compete. Many low-end devices still run 32-bit apps.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Telemetry that makes triage possible
Thread.setDefaultUncaughtExceptionHandler { t, e ->
    if (e is OutOfMemoryError) {
        val rt = Runtime.getRuntime()
        report("oom", mapOf(
            "msg" to e.message?.take(200),
            "javaUsedMb" to (rt.totalMemory() - rt.freeMemory()) shr 20,
            "maxMb" to rt.maxMemory() shr 20,
            "threads" to Thread.getAllStackTraces().size,
            "nativeKb" to Debug.getNativeHeapAllocatedSize() / 1024,
            "fds" to File("/proc/self/fd").list()?.size))
    }
    previousHandler?.uncaughtException(t, e)
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Catching OutOfMemoryError and carrying on; state may be corrupt. Only catch it around a single optional allocation (e.g., decode a thumbnail) and degrade gracefully.
  • Grouping all OOMs into one issue in the crash dashboard.
  • Not recording thread count and FD count at crash time.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Which of these produce no stack trace? → LMK kills, and native aborts (you get tombstones/Play Console native crash data, not Java stacks).
  2. How do you monitor LMK kills? → ApplicationExitInfo on next launch (API 30+).
  3. Thread OOM with only 500 threads, why? → Each thread reserves virtual space (1 MB Java stack + guard); with other mappings in a 32-bit address space it can exhaust before the memory is "used". Also cgroup pids.max can cap it.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "OOM means too much memory, use less bitmap." Senior: classifies by signature, extracts info from the message numbers, instruments telemetry to disambiguate, and picks the fix per class.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team spent a sprint shrinking images for an OOM cluster whose message was pthread_create failed; the cause was an unbounded thread pool.

questions.contextHtml:
A video-and-photo sharing app is expanding to a new market. DAU goes from 800k to 8M over 3 months. Device mix in the new market: 62% have 2 GB RAM or less, many on Android 9 to 11 Go-edition-like builds, 32-bit userspace common. Existing numbers: crash-free users 99.4% overall, but in the new market 96.8%. Of crashes there, 58% are OutOfMemoryError. A sample message:

java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Failed to allocate a 14745616 byte allocation with 2097152 free bytes and 3MB until OOM, target footprint 134217728, growth limit 134217728 at ImageFilters.applyVignette(ImageFilters.kt:41), called from the "edit photo" screen. The product team wants to "just set largeHeap and ship".
questions.promptHtml: How do you drive the OOM rate in the new market down without degrading the flagship experience?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add largeHeap and compress images more." Doesn't read the message, doesn't segment by device, and treats the problem as one global setting.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which screens and what share of the 58% sit in the edit screen? (Concentration decides the fix.) What is the maximum photo resolution accepted from the camera and gallery? (Defines worst-case arrays.) Is the filter code Java arrays or RenderScript/GPU? (RenderScript is deprecated since API 31.) What are p50 and p90 memoryClass values in this cohort? (Real cap, not marketing RAM.) Are crashes spiking with session length or at first filter use? (Leak vs peak.)
  2. Immediate mitigation: Remote-config cap the edit resolution to 1280 px longest edge for devices with memoryClass <= 192 or isLowRamDevice; keep original on disk for upload. No largeHeap as the first move.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Peak allocation: the int[] of 1920x1920 = 14.7 MB plus working copies, with a 128 MB cap and ~130 MB live from other things. (b) Multiple full-resolution copies alive (original decode, filter input, filter output, undo stack): 4 x 14.7 MB = 59 MB. (c) Leaks across edits (bitmap held in ViewModel plus Activity). (d) Image cache sized by a constant, not by memoryClass.
  4. How I'd verify each: Reproduce on a physical 2 GB device or emulator with -memory and a 128 MB heap; heap dump while at the filter screen; Memory Profiler allocation tracking during "apply filter"; check the target footprint number in the message equals maxMemory, confirming the cap is 128 MB (134,217,728 = 128 x 1,048,576).
  5. Root cause: The filter allocates full-resolution IntArray buffers on the Java heap, 14.7 MB each, with multiple copies, on a 128 MB cap. At ~118 MB live plus one allocation of 14.7 MB, it fails. On flagships (cap 384 to 512 MB) the same code passes.
  6. Fix: Short-term: tiered limits and downsampled editing preview, full-resolution only at export in strips. Long-term: process in tiles (e.g., 512x512 strips) reusing one buffer; use GPU shaders (RenderEffect API 31+, or OpenGL/AGSL on API 33+) so pixels never enter Java arrays; reuse a bitmap pool.
val tier = when {
    am.isLowRamDevice || am.memoryClass <= 128 -> 1024
    am.memoryClass <= 256 -> 1600
    else -> 2400
}
val bmp = decodeScaledTo(uri, maxEdge = tier)
  1. Prevention: Device-tier test lab including 1 to 2 GB devices; release gate on OOM rate per memoryClass bucket; log memoryClass as a custom Crashlytics key; staged rollout by country.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do (and why): I would not ship largeHeap as the plan: bigger heap means slower GC and higher LMK kill likelihood, which hurts a cohort already memory-starved. I would not drop quality for everyone; tiering protects flagships. I would not detect "low-end" by RAM marketing size alone; use memoryClass and isLowRamDevice.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Product refuses lower resolution on low-end. → Offer "high quality" export that processes in tiles server-side or on-device in strips; preview stays low-res.
  • After the fix, background kills spike. → Footprint is still too high while cached. Trim caches at UI_HIDDEN and avoid retaining editor state in memory; persist drafts.
  • Can I detect device capability server-side? → Send tier in headers; but device-side gating is the source of truth since memoryClass is only known on-device.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite from an emerging-market launch: the team added largeHeap first and OOM dropped 12%, then crash-free recovered only after tiling; the surprise was that low-end users were worse off with largeHeap due to more background kills.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Suggests largeHeap globally; no data segmentation.
  • Hire: Reads the message, identifies the array, segments by memoryClass, tiers resolution.
  • Strong hire: Does the math (14.7 MB x copies vs 128 MB), proposes tiling/GPU, defines device-tier monitoring and a staged rollout.

questions.promptHtml: A user's app has a flat Java heap but total memory keeps rising and the OS eventually kills it. How do you determine whether native memory is the cause, and what are the common native-side leaks in an Android app?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests depth past the Java heap: tools for native and graphics memory, and awareness of non-obvious native consumers.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: I compare dumpsys meminfo rows over time: if Native Heap or Graphics grows while Java Heap stays flat, it's native or graphics. Common sources are direct ByteBuffers, bitmap pixels, JNI/NDK code that never frees, unclosed Cursors or media codecs/players, and third-party SDK native libraries. To find the allocation sites I use the native memory profiler (heapprofd under Perfetto, via Android Studio's Native Memory Profiler on Android 10+).

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Native heap is process malloc memory, served by the system allocator (Scudo is the default allocator for apps from Android 11; earlier jemalloc). Not tracked by the Java GC; it grows until freed explicitly or by a Java-side owner.
  • Java objects can own native memory: Bitmap (pixels, API 26+), ByteBuffer.allocateDirect, Cursor (CursorWindow ashmem), MediaCodec, Surface, Parcel, SQLiteDatabase. They free it only when closed or when the Java wrapper becomes unreachable and the cleaner runs. Leaking the wrapper (an Activity leak holding a codec) leaks the native memory too, with little Java footprint.
  • NativeAllocationRegistry (hidden API used by framework classes) lets ART account native bytes so GC can trigger earlier; third-party code usually can't rely on it.
  • Direct ByteBuffers: allocateDirect(64 MB) does not count against the Java cap, but the JVM may call System.gc() when too much is outstanding. Large short-lived direct buffers cause native RSS spikes.
  • Sequence to localize:
1. dumpsys meminfo   -> which row grows (Native? Graphics? Code? Other?)
2. Native row grows  -> heapprofd: callstacks of live allocations by size
3. Graphics grows    -> check bitmaps / textures / SurfaceViews / WebView
4. Other/ashmem      -> CursorWindows, memfd, shared memory

  • Never closing Cursor/MediaCodec/ParcelFileDescriptor; relying on finalization.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you tell if a third-party SDK leaks native memory? → Run the app with and without the SDK in a soak test and compare Native Heap slope; heapprofd callstacks show the library's .so.
  2. What tool catches heap corruption (use-after-free) rather than leaks? → HWASan/ASan builds, GWP-ASan (opt-in per app via manifest, Android 11+), MTE on supported hardware.
  3. Why can't I use Runtime.maxMemory() to guard native usage? → It only reflects the Java cap; use Debug.getNativeHeapAllocatedSize() and ActivityManager.MemoryInfo for budgets.

questions.promptHtml: How is ART's modern garbage collector designed to keep pauses short, and how has the collector changed across Android releases? What would a senior app engineer need to know about it?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests depth beyond "GC is automatic": the cost model, why allocation rate matters, and awareness of platform evolution.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: ART moved from Dalvik's stop-the-world mark-sweep, to concurrent mark-sweep, to the Concurrent Copying (CC) collector as default in Android 8.0. CC copies live objects out of fragmented regions while the app runs, using read barriers so threads see consistent references, which keeps pauses tiny and compacts the heap. Android 14 introduced a userfaultfd-based Concurrent Mark-Compact collector on supported kernels, and newer releases continue to add generational behavior. Exact release/default status changes, so I verify against current AOSP and release notes. For app code the takeaways are: allocation rate matters more than pauses, and large objects and native pressure are handled differently.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Dalvik: stop-the-world mark-sweep; 10 to 100 ms pauses; non-moving heap, fragmentation.
  • ART (5.0 to 7.x): concurrent mark-sweep, a compacting "background" collector when the app goes to background (to reduce footprint), shorter pauses but fragmentation in foreground.
  • Concurrent Copying (Android 8.0 / API 26): region-based heap. Collector marks, then copies live objects from regions to new regions, concurrently with mutators. A read barrier on reference loads in app code (JIT/AOT-inserted) ensures a thread never sees an object in an inconsistent state. Pauses are essentially sub-millisecond to low milliseconds and independent of heap size. Cost: a small overhead on reference loads and extra CPU on GC threads.
  • Concurrent Mark-Compact (Android 14 / API 34): uses Linux userfaultfd to compact in place concurrently; reduces memory overhead vs copying (less to-space reserve). Requires kernel support; otherwise CC remains. Generational variants have been rolling out; exact versions and defaults: verify on source.android.com / AOSP.
  • Heap spaces: image space (boot image, shared), zygote space, main region space for app objects, large object space (LOS) for big arrays/strings (threshold 12 KB; allocated and freed separately, not copied), non-moving space for objects that can't move.
  • Triggers: allocation failure, concurrent threshold (based on target utilization), native allocation notifications (bitmaps in native memory register their size), explicit calls.
  • Why pauses aren't the story: barrier overhead, GC thread CPU use on little cores, and blocking collections (when allocator waits) are the user-visible costs.
Mutator threads  ---- run ---- run ---- run ---- (read barrier on loads)
GC thread        ====== mark ====== copy live regions ====== free from-space
Pauses           |a| (small)        |b|

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Quoting "GC pauses 100 ms" from Dalvik era blogs for modern devices.
  • Assuming largeHeap, pooling, or System.gc() always help.
  • Stating the exact Android version and default for generational/CMC as certain without checking; behavior depends on kernel and OEM.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why do large arrays live in a separate space? → Copying multi-MB arrays is expensive; LOS objects aren't moved.
  2. Does WeakReference/SoftReference interplay with GC? → Soft refs are cleared under pressure per policy; Android recommends against soft-reference caches (use LruCache).
  3. Why can GC be slower on small cores? → Concurrent GC threads run on whatever cores are available; on loaded little cores marking takes longer, extending the window where allocation could stall.
