questions.contextHtml: A delivery-rider app (400k riders, shifts last 6 to 8 hours, mostly 3 GB devices with memoryClass 256). After release 8.4: support reports "app freezes and then restarts after about 45 to 90 minutes", and rating drops from 4.4 to 4.0. Crashlytics: OOM rate from 0.3% to 2.1% of sessions, but sessions shorter than 20 minutes are unaffected. Heap used after "Force GC" in a staging soak: 92 MB at 0 min, 147 MB at 30 min, 202 MB at 60 min, i.e., +1.8 MB/min. The release also added: live map markers per delivery, a retry wrapper around location updates, an RxJava stream for order status, and a debug-only logger that was left enabled by mistake. LeakCanary is only in debug builds and reports no Activity leaks.
questions.promptHtml: Walk me through diagnosis and fix. Why did LeakCanary say clean, and why does it only show up late in the shift?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Run LeakCanary, fix the leaks, increase heap." Doesn't explain the missing Activity leak, doesn't compute time-to-OOM, and ignores non-Activity leaks (growing collections, subscriptions).

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which screen is open during the 45 to 90 minutes (a single long-lived Activity)? Is the crash tied to time in app or number of events (location pings, order updates)? Which build flag differences exist between release and the soak build? Did the OOM Java message show large or small allocation (cliff vs big alloc)? Does the issue appear in background FGS time too?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Ship a flag to stop the extra logger, cap in-memory marker/polyline history, and force-restart a degraded map screen after N minutes if memory telemetry exceeds a threshold. Rollback 8.4 to the stable channel if the staged rollout hasn't completed.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Unbounded growth of a list (location track points, markers) in a singleton or ViewModel: leak of data, not of an Activity. (b) A subscription created on each onResume/reconnect and never disposed, so N duplicate observers retain closures. (c) A new BitmapDescriptor/marker bitmap created per location update. (d) The leftover logger buffering messages in memory. (e) Native growth (map SDK tiles cache), which Java Heap doesn't show.
  4. How I'd verify each: Math first: headroom is 256 - 92 = 164 MB; at 1.8 MB/min that is ~91 min to the cap, with GC thrash starting around 80% (~205 MB at ~60 min). That matches the "45 to 90 min" report, so a steady linear leak, not a spike. Heap dump at 0 min and 40 min in the same screen, diff in Memory Profiler: sort by retained size and count growth. Expect something like 12,000 instances of LatLng/Marker/LogEntry. Check dumpsys meminfo Native/Graphics rows too, to rule out (e).
  5. Root cause: Two things stacked: marker/track history appended on each location update (every 3 s = 1,200/hour) without trimming, and a debug logger storing every line (long strings, about 0.5 KB each) in a list. 1,200/h x 3 KB per marker/point/description objects ≈ 3.6 MB/h doesn't alone explain 108 MB/h; the retry wrapper re-subscribed on each failure and left 1 closure with the previous track list attached, multiplying retained copies. Multiple small leaks summing to +1.8 MB/min. LeakCanary was clean because no Activity/Fragment/View/ViewModel was held after destruction. The screen never gets destroyed during a shift, so there is nothing to "leak"; the structure is a live-screen growth bug.
  6. Fix: Bound history (ring buffer of last 200 points), dispose subscription before resubscribing (CompositeDisposable.clear() or repeatOnLifecycle flows), reuse one BitmapDescriptor per marker type, remove the logger from release (BuildConfig.DEBUG or R8 -assumenosideeffects for log calls).
class Track(private val max: Int = 200) {
    private val points = ArrayDeque<LatLng>(max)
    fun add(p: LatLng) { if (points.size == max) points.removeFirst(); points.addLast(p) }
}
private val markerIcon by lazy { BitmapDescriptorFactory.fromResource(R.drawable.rider) } // once
  1. Prevention: Soak test in CI (2-hour monkey or scripted flow with periodic heap capture and a slope assertion, e.g., < 0.2 MB/min); ship Debug.getRuntimeStat heap-after-GC samples as telemetry every 5 minutes with session time; alert on p95 slope; review checklist: "any collection in a long-lived scope has a bound".
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do (and why): I'd not raise largeHeap: it converts a 90-minute crash into a 180-minute one without telling us why, and rider devices have little spare RAM. I'd not force periodic System.gc(), which doesn't free reachable data. I'd not rely on LeakCanary alone for this class of bug.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Heap diff shows nothing big, yet native grows. → Check the map SDK's tile/bitmap cache and Graphics row; set the SDK cache limits; use heapprofd.
  • Can't reproduce on a developer's flagship. → Cap is larger and it takes longer; reproduce on a 256 MB-class device or emulator with a 256 MB cap and accelerate by simulating location pings at 10x.
  • Fix shipped but 1% OOM remains. → Look at the OOM message for other classes (pthread, native) and at cohorts (OS version/OEM).

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite of a logistics app: the real culprit was a retry wrapper that kept previous subscriptions alive; the metric that finally caught it was "heap after GC vs minutes in session" plotted per release, which turned a vague "freezes sometimes" ticket into a precise slope.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Run LeakCanary, increase heap; can't explain the clean result.
  • Hire: Computes time-to-OOM from slope, diffs heap dumps, finds unbounded collections and undisposed subscriptions.
  • Strong hire: Explains why Activity-leak tools miss it, adds slope-based telemetry and soak-test gates, and bounds long-lived structures by design.

questions.contextHtml:
A photo-feed app (6M DAU) uses a hand-rolled LruCache<String, Bitmap> fixed at 64 MB. Device spread: 35% have memoryClass 128 or less, 45% have 192 to 256, 20% have 384+. Thumbnails are 400x400 ARGB_8888. OOM is 1.4% of sessions on low devices, while on flagships scrolling re-decodes images constantly (cache hit rate 38%) because 64 MB is too small for their big grids. The code:

val cache = object : LruCache<String, Bitmap>(64 * 1024 * 1024) {
    override fun sizeOf(key: String, v: Bitmap) = 1   // bug: counts entries, not bytes
}

Product wants one setting that works for everyone.
questions.promptHtml: Design the cache sizing. What is wrong with the current code, and how do you pick numbers?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Make it 1/8 of memory." Doesn't notice sizeOf returns 1 (so the cache holds 64M entries, i.e., unbounded), ignores that pixels are native on API 26+ so the Java cap doesn't protect you, and ignores low-RAM tiers.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is there also a disk cache and a second library cache (Glide/Coil) stacked on top? What are screen sizes and image display sizes? What min API (pixels native vs Java heap)? Is the same process shared by other memory-heavy features? What hit-rate and OOM targets exist?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Fix sizeOf to return allocationByteCount and set a sane max so the cache stops being unbounded.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) The sizeOf bug makes the "64 MB" a 64-million-entry limit, so low devices OOM. (b) Even a correct 64 MB is too big where the Java cap is 128 MB combined with other heap use. (c) On flagships, an overly small fixed budget gives the low hit rate. (d) Duplicate caches (library + custom) double the cost.
  4. How I'd verify each: Heap dump on a low device: count Bitmap instances and total retained; metric for hit rate vs cache size by device tier; log cache.size() vs memoryClass.
  5. Root cause: Wrong unit in sizeOf plus a fixed constant instead of a tier-derived budget.
  6. Fix: Size by bytes and derive from memoryClass, clamp by tier. Math: a 400x400 ARGB_8888 thumbnail is 400 x 400 x 4 = 640,000 bytes (about 625 KiB). A budget of memoryClass/8: 128 MB class → 16 MB → ~26 thumbs; 256 MB class → 32 MB → ~52 thumbs; 512 MB class → 64 MB → ~104 thumbs. Too few for big grids, so on large screens also decode thumbs smaller (display-size-bound) or use RGB_565 for opaque images (half the bytes, doubling the count).
val am = context.getSystemService(ActivityManager::class.java)
val fraction = if (am.isLowRamDevice) 0.10 else 0.15
val bytes = (am.memoryClass * 1024L * 1024L * fraction).toLong().coerceIn(8L shl 20, 96L shl 20).toInt()
val cache = object : LruCache<String, Bitmap>(bytes) {
    override fun sizeOf(key: String, v: Bitmap) = v.allocationByteCount
}
// trim under pressure
override fun onTrimMemory(level: Int) {
    if (level >= ComponentCallbacks2.TRIM_MEMORY_BACKGROUND) cache.evictAll()
    else if (level >= ComponentCallbacks2.TRIM_MEMORY_UI_HIDDEN) cache.trimToSize(cache.size() / 2)
}
  1. Prevention: Unit test sizeOf units; dashboard of hit rate and OOM by memoryClass bucket; a rule that cache budgets derive from device class, never constants.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do (and why): I'd not use SoftReference caches (cleared unpredictably, discouraged on Android). I'd not make the budget a large fraction of maxMemory since pixels are native on API 26+ and are not stopped by the Java cap, so total process footprint and LMK risk matter, not just OOM. I'd not keep a custom cache if the image library already has a tuned one; I'd configure it instead.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Hardware bitmaps enabled: what changes in accounting? → Pixels are in graphics memory; allocationByteCount still approximates the cost, but check the Graphics row too.
  • Memory Class lies on some OEMs. → Treat as a prior; use ActivityManager.MemoryInfo.totalMem and adaptive trimming from trim callbacks and exit-info telemetry.
  • Hit rate still low on grids. → Scale-aware decode (smaller thumbs), prefetch window, disk cache for decode-free reads.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite of a feed app: a cache sized by "number of entries" worked for months on 3 GB devices and failed only when a redesign doubled the thumbnail size; the unit bug had been masked by small images.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Picks a constant; misses the sizeOf bug.
  • Hire: Fixes units, derives from memoryClass, adds trim handling.
  • Strong hire: Does the per-thumbnail math, reasons about native pixel memory and LMK, tiers by device, and measures hit rate vs OOM.

questions.contextHtml:
Post-incident review for release 5.7. Within 6 hours of 20% rollout, crash-free users fell from 99.3% to 98.1%. The top new issue (0.9% of sessions):

java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: pthread_create (1040KB stack) failed: Try again
    at java.lang.Thread.nativeCreate(Native Method)
    at java.lang.Thread.start(Thread.java:1063)
    at java.util.concurrent.ThreadPoolExecutor.addWorker(ThreadPoolExecutor.java:957)
    at com.example.net.Prefetcher.fetch(Prefetcher.kt:58)

Devices: 78% are 32-bit-process devices with 2 to 3 GB RAM. The Java heap at crash time is 70 to 110 MB with maxMemory 256 MB. The release added an image prefetcher for the feed. Dashboards for heap OOM were green.

fun fetch(urls: List<String>) {
    urls.forEach { u ->
        Executors.newCachedThreadPool().execute { download(u) }   // new pool per URL
    }
}
questions.promptHtml: Run the post-incident review: what happened, why heap telemetry didn't warn you, and what changes.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Memory leak, reduce heap." Ignores that the Java heap was fine, and doesn't understand threads as a resource with their own limit.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: How many URLs per fetch call and how often? Do downloads block long (slow networks)? Did other libraries also create threads? Is the pool ever shut down? What is the thread count distribution at crash?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Halt the rollout, remote-flag the prefetcher off, and push a patch using a shared bounded executor. Add thread count to crash keys.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Thread explosion from per-call pools with idle threads kept alive (cached pool threads linger 60 s, and on slow networks downloads hold threads longer). (b) Virtual address space exhaustion in 32-bit processes (each Java thread reserves about 1 MB stack plus guard). (c) Per-process or cgroup thread limits on some OEMs. (d) Thread leak elsewhere (a library).
  4. How I'd verify each: Math: 40 URLs per feed page x 5 pages scrolled in a minute = 200 pools, each spawning a thread that stays 60 s idle plus download time: ~200 threads x ~1 MB = ~200 MB of address space just in stacks, on top of the 256 MB heap, mapped libs, and graphics mappings in a ~3 GB 32-bit address space. Check: reproduce with scripted scroll on a 32-bit 2 GB device, watch adb shell ls /proc/<pid>/task | wc -l and grep Threads /proc/<pid>/status; dumpsys meminfo Stack row; thread dump (kill -3 or Thread.getAllStackTraces()) grouped by name to see 'pool-N-thread-1' repeated.
  5. Root cause: A new executor per URL: each newCachedThreadPool() creates a separate pool that is never shut down, so threads multiply with scrolling. The failure is a thread-creation failure (virtual memory and OS limits), not heap exhaustion, so heap dashboards stayed green.
  6. Fix: One shared, bounded executor (or coroutines on Dispatchers.IO.limitedParallelism(4)), cancellation tied to screen scope, and request coalescing.
private val io = Dispatchers.IO.limitedParallelism(4)
fun fetch(scope: CoroutineScope, urls: List<String>) = urls.forEach { u -> scope.launch(io) { download(u) } }
  1. Prevention: Thread count and FD count as crash keys and a debug-build watchdog (alert when Thread.activeCount exceeds 100); StrictMode detectLeakedClosableObjects (and ThreadPolicy for main-thread work); lint/review rule against Executors.new* inside functions; classify OOM signatures separately on the dashboard; load test on 32-bit low-memory devices before 100%.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do (and why): I would not just lower pthread stack size (not settable per normal Java thread reliably and fragile). I would not raise heap. I'd not remove prefetching: it was a product win; I'd bound and prioritize it.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why did only 78% of crashes come from 32-bit devices? → Address space is the bottleneck there; 64-bit processes hit pid/cgroup limits much later.
  • Dispatchers.IO caps at 64 threads (default), so is that safe? → Better than unbounded; still, limitedParallelism per feature stops one feature from starving others.
  • What would you add to the staged rollout? → Gate promotion on thread-count p99 and OOM signature rate.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite of a news app: a crash cluster was triaged as "heap OOM" for two sprints because both messages start with OutOfMemoryError. The thread count crash key resolved it in an hour.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Treats it as a heap leak.
  • Hire: Identifies thread explosion from per-call executors, bounds the pool.
  • Strong hire: Explains address-space math, adds telemetry and rollout gates, and classifies OOM signatures.

questions.contextHtml: The PM writes: "Our new market uses cheap phones, make the app work well on 1 GB devices." No further details. Current numbers on devices with isLowRamDevice == true (about 9% of users): cold start p50 3.4 s vs 1.6 s on others, 7-day retention 8 points lower, crash-free 98.2% vs 99.5%, 40% of sessions end with REASON_LOW_MEMORY in exit info. Engineering team is 6 people, one quarter.
questions.promptHtml: How do you turn this into a plan?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Optimize memory everywhere and use less images." No definition of "well", no baseline, no prioritization.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What does "work well" mean: crash-free, startup, smoothness, retention? What devices precisely (RAM, Android Go edition, API level, CPU)? Is feature parity required or can features degrade? What is the budget in engineering and APK size? What are the revenue stakes for this cohort?
  2. Immediate mitigation: No incident, so first measure. Within a week: tag all telemetry with isLowRamDevice, memoryClass, totalMem; start recording exit reasons; take PSS baselines on a real 1 GB device in key flows.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Foreground footprint exceeds what the device can keep alongside system services, causing thrash and slow starts. (b) Background footprint too large, so we're killed often and lose state, causing cold starts (explains 40% LMK exits and 3.4 s start). (c) A few heavy features (video, large images, WebView, many SDKs initialized at startup). (d) Multiple processes or services increase total.
  4. How I'd verify each: dumpsys meminfo PSS on a 1 GB device in main flows; Perfetto trace for startup and memory counters (mem.rss per process); compare cached-process PSS with the typical (target maybe < 60 MB when backgrounded; set budgets from measurement); ApplicationExitInfo by importance; startup SDK init audit.
  5. Root cause: Unknown at the start; likely a mix of large background footprint and heavy initialization. I'd say so and let data rank the work.
  6. Fix: Define a written budget: foreground PSS ≤ X MB, backgrounded PSS ≤ Y MB, cold start ≤ Z s on a reference device, crash-free ≥ 99%. Then: a low-RAM mode behind isLowRamDevice (smaller image tiers, no autoplay, lighter animations, disabled prefetch), release caches at TRIM_MEMORY_UI_HIDDEN, lazy-init SDKs, restore state fast after kill, and consider an app variant or Android Go-optimized build if needed. Android Go devices are generally 2 GB or less RAM with a lighter OS configuration.
object Tier { fun low(ctx: Context) =
    ctx.getSystemService(ActivityManager::class.java).isLowRamDevice }
  1. Prevention: A reference low-RAM device in CI/perf lab; memory regression gate on PSS in key flows; budgets in the PR template; dashboards by tier.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do (and why): Not largeHeap. Not a separate codebase fork. Not "optimize everything": 6 people, one quarter means picking 3 flows covering most usage. I'd negotiate feature degradation (video quality, animations) explicitly with the PM.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• PM wants video autoplay kept. → Offer cap resolution, one player instance, release on UI_HIDDEN, and show data.
  • Start time remains slow after memory work. → It's cold-start work: defer init, baseline profiles (A6 owns the practice).
  • How do you know it worked? → Exit reasons share of LMK, cold-start rate, p50 start, retention on the cohort.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite from a lite-market push: the biggest win was not a memory trick but removing three SDKs initialized at startup, which cut cold PSS by 35 MB and made the app survive in the background twice as long.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Starts coding optimizations immediately.
  • Hire: Asks for definitions, measures baselines, sets budgets.
  • Strong hire: Separates foreground vs cached footprint, uses exit-info and tiering, scopes the quarter, and negotiates trade-offs with product.

questions.contextHtml:
A finance app's "export transactions" fetches up to 80 MB of JSON (about 400k records) and stores it for offline search. In production, 1.1% of sessions that use it OOM on devices with memoryClass 256; p95 time for the screen is 14 s. Current code:

val body = client.newCall(req).execute().body!!.string()          // 80 MB
val list: List<Txn> = Gson().fromJson(body, object : TypeToken<List<Txn>>() {}.type)
dao.insertAll(list)

Stack: OutOfMemoryError: Failed to allocate a 167772176 byte allocation with 18874368 free bytes and 18MB until OOM in okio.Buffer/String creation.
questions.promptHtml: Explain the failure with numbers and redesign it.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Paginate the API" (maybe right, but no explanation of the peak) or "use largeHeap".

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Can the server paginate or provide NDJSON? Do we need all records at once? What is the target device floor? Is offline search required over the whole set? Is the payload compressed on the wire?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Server-side or client-side cap (e.g., last 12 months) behind a flag, and show a progress UI; stop .string().
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Peak memory from holding the payload multiple times. (b) Parsed object graph larger than the JSON text (per-record objects, strings, boxed numbers). (c) Single huge allocation hitting the LOS (167,772,176 bytes = 160 MiB: the string/char array buffer being copied while growing).
  4. How I'd verify each: Heap dump during parse; allocation tracking shows byte[]/char[]/String of 80 to 160 MB; compute peak.
  5. Root cause: Peak math. The body bytes are buffered (80 MB); converting to a String creates another buffer of 80 MB (or up to 160 MB if two bytes/char) while the first is alive; Gson then builds 400k objects. Even at 200 bytes per record plus strings, parsed data is ~80 to 160 MB. Peak of 80 + 160 + 120 = ~360 MB against a 256 MB cap. The final failed allocation (160 MiB) is the string copy.
  6. Fix: Stream: never materialize the body; parse incrementally and insert in batches.
client.newCall(req).execute().use { resp ->
    resp.body!!.source().inputStream().bufferedReader().use { r ->
        val reader = JsonReader(r)                 // com.google.gson.stream.JsonReader
        reader.beginArray()
        val batch = ArrayList<Txn>(500)
        while (reader.hasNext()) {
            batch += gson.fromJson<Txn>(reader, Txn::class.java)
            if (batch.size == 500) { dao.insertAll(batch); batch.clear() }
        }
        reader.endArray()
        if (batch.isNotEmpty()) dao.insertAll(batch)
    }
}

Peak becomes a 500-record batch (about 100 KB) plus buffers. Long term: paginated or delta sync API, gzip, and search through the database (FTS) rather than in memory. 7. Prevention: Lint/review ban on .string() for unbounded responses; a test with a synthetic 100 MB payload on a low-memory emulator; payload size histogram in telemetry. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do (and why): I'd not use largeHeap (peak still scales with payload). Streaming loses atomicity (partial import): use a transaction or staging table and swap. I'd not compress in memory.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Do batch inserts in Room need a transaction? → Yes, wrap in @Transaction or withTransaction for atomicity and speed (A5 owns Room depth).
  • What if the server cannot change? → Streaming still works with the existing array response; the parse is the same.
  • What about kotlinx.serialization? → decodeToSequence on a stream works for top-level arrays (verify the library version in use).

  • Hire: Identifies multiple copies, streams the parse.

questions.contextHtml: To cut graphics+native memory, the team plans to enable hardware bitmaps for all image loads (Coil/Glide default flipped) in an app with 15M DAU. Test results: median PSS down 18% on image-heavy screens. Concerns from QA: "share as image", the color-accent feature (Palette), and the profile photo blur may break. Android 8.0 and 8.1 make up 4% of users. You have a 2-week window and a 5%-10%-50%-100% staged rollout.
questions.promptHtml: How do you migrate safely?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Flip it and watch Crashlytics." No inventory of pixel-reading code paths and no cohort guardrails.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which code reads pixels or draws into a software canvas? Is there a single image-loading entry point? Which API levels are in scope? Do we have remote config at the call site level? What metrics define success (PSS, OOM, crash-free)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Not an incident; set up the kill switch first: a remote flag read at image request time.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Features that call getPixel, Palette, blur transformations, Canvas(bitmap) drawing, bitmap.compress fail. (b) Software-canvas screenshot/export paths fail (Software rendering doesn't support hardware bitmaps). (c) On Android 8.0/8.1, hardware bitmaps consumed file descriptors and could hit the FD limit under many images. (d) Memory win smaller than lab due to double accounting (graphics memory not in your Java dashboards).
  4. How I'd verify each: Grep for getPixel, Palette.from, Canvas(, copyPixelsTo, Transformation, compress(; instrumented UI tests on those screens; run with the flag on in internal builds and adb shell dumpsys meminfo Graphics row; ls /proc/<pid>/fd | wc -l on 8.0 devices; exceptions grouped by message.
  5. Root cause: The migration risk is capability loss: hardware bitmaps are GPU-only and immutable, so every CPU-side consumer is a landmine; plus the FD behavior on 8.x.
  6. Fix: Opt-in per request, default on for plain display, explicit opt-out where pixels are needed, and a safety net.
// Display-only request keeps hardware
imageView.load(url)                                  // allowHardware default true in Coil
// Pixel consumers opt out
imageView.load(url) { allowHardware(false) }
// Safety net: copy before reading
fun Bitmap.readable(): Bitmap =
    if (config == Bitmap.Config.HARDWARE) copy(Bitmap.Config.ARGB_8888, false) else this

Disable hardware for API 26/27 via the flag if FD usage is high. 7. Prevention: Lint/review checklist for bitmap consumers; UI tests on share/blur/Palette flows; dashboards slicing crashes by exception message and API level; keep the flag permanent. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do (and why): I'd not enable globally on day one; the 18% PSS gain doesn't justify a possible 2% crash spike on key features. I'd not strip the safety copy() since it temporarily raises memory; use it only on those paths. I'd not trust lab PSS alone: compare field Graphics-memory telemetry and LMK exit share.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• 10% stage shows crashes in a third-party carousel library. → Disable hardware for those views via per-request flag, file an issue, and keep the rollout paused.
  • Memory improved but jank increased on old GPUs. → Check texture upload behavior on those devices; segment by GPU and fall back by device class.
  • How do you prove the win? → Field metrics: LMK exit share and OOM rate by cohort, not only lab PSS.

sections.html: A composite from a social app: the rollout stalled at 5% when a share-as-image feature crashed; the team had listed it in advance, so the fix was a one-line opt-out and the rollout resumed the same day.

sections.html:
• No hire: Flips globally.
  • Hire: Inventories pixel consumers, uses a flag and staged rollout.
  • Strong hire: Handles 8.x FD risk, per-request opt-outs, field metrics for success, and keeps the kill switch.
